title: Come unto me (Matthew 11:25–30)
hookLine: a week too heavy, and an invitation to take on a yoke
tomorrow: what do you do with something that's already cracked?

lines: THE LIST IS LONGER THAN THE WEEK.
cards: Two tests, a shift, rehearsal every night, and a phone that buzzes through dinner. Some weeks the list is longer than the week. Here's the surprise in Jesus' answer to heavy.
He doesn't say: put everything down. He says: take my yoke. A yoke is a wooden beam that sits across the necks of working animals so they can pull together.
It's the gear of work, not of rest. So Christians read his offer in more than one way.

teach.b: Here are his words, in the King James: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."
One reading leans on the first sentence.

teach.h: REST AS A GIFT: I WILL GIVE YOU.
teach.b: Rest is a gift: I will give you rest. Nobody earns it. You come tired, as you are, and it's handed to you.

Just before this, Jesus thanks his Father for showing these things to babes, not to the wise and prudent, and babes don't earn anything. Another reading leans on the second sentence. Take my yoke, and learn of me.
A yoke is still a yoke. The rest comes from pulling beside a gentle teacher, learning his pace, not from never pulling again. On this reading, rest is something you find along the way.

teach.h: REST AS A PATH: LEARN OF ME.
teach.b: Notice that the verses hold both verbs: I will give you rest, and ye shall find rest. Christians who stress either one are quoting the same lines. And the words of the promise are older than Matthew.

teach.h: GIVE AND FIND, IN ONE BREATH.
teach.b: Jeremiah, in the King James: "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls."

how: Some Christians pray Matthew 11:28 at the end of a hard day, and in some churches the words come unto me are read aloud near communion as an invitation.

o: an open invitation to the tired to find rest
a command to come to the temple to pray
a call only for those who are already wise

games.q: the easy yoke — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus promises his followers no burden at all
he says my burden is light, not that there is none. the yoke is still a yoke.
Jesus describes himself in this passage
"I am meek and lowly in heart."
a yoke is a picture of lying down to rest
a yoke is the beam working animals pull with. the rest comes while pulling beside someone gentle.

games.q: a friend says: rest is pure gift, you just come; the yoke part is extra. give the best case for the other side.
o: rest is earned: the harder you work, the more God gives you.
he says take my yoke and learn of me: rest is found walking his way.
the yoke means church rules, and rest comes once you keep them all.
games.why: the strongest case for the second reading quotes the text itself: take my yoke, and learn of me, and ye shall find rest. the first reading quotes the line before it: I will give you rest. both are in Matthew 11.

practice: Let your shoulders drop, and rest your hands open on your knees, palms up, as if you've just set something down. Name one weight you're carrying this week, one task, one worry, one person you're holding up.
For the length of the sit, leave it there in your open hands, and let someone else hold the other end of the beam.

wordCard.voice: Come unto me. The open door of Matthew 11: no test, no list, only tired people and an offer of rest.

orig.note: Greek: easy, good, kind. Matthew 11:30: my yoke is easy.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: rest for your souls, given and found, under a yoke made for two. Be well.
